lessons.title: Receivables Ageing, Collections and Bad Debt Control

children.text: Your receivables are ₹58 crore and your debtor days are 118. Those two numbers are the ones that reach the board. Neither of them tells you whether ₹3 crore of that book will never be collected, and that is the only part that actually costs you money.
This lesson is about the schedule underneath the total, the process that keeps it healthy, and what to do in India when a customer simply stops paying.
The Ageing Schedule Is the Real Report
An
ageing schedule
splits the book by how overdue each invoice is. Here is the Sunrise Ceramics book you have seen since Chapter 1, aged properly.

markDefs.definition: A schedule that splits the receivable book by how long each invoice has been outstanding, instead of showing one total.

stats.label: Not yet due
stats.context: 44.83% of the book, which is the only genuinely healthy part

stats.label: Over 90 days
stats.context: 12.07% of the book, where collection probability falls sharply

stats.label: Days beyond terms
stats.context: The weighted average overdue age across the whole book

children.text: Now compare two companies that both report ₹58 crore of receivables and identical debtor days. One has ₹30 crore not due, ₹20 crore under 30 days and ₹8 crore in the 31 to 60 bucket, with nothing older. The other is the book above, with ₹7 crore beyond 90 days. Same
DSO
, completely different businesses. The average hides the tail, and the tail is where the loss lives.

markDefs.definition: Days Sales Outstanding. Receivables divided by sales, times 365. An average, which tells you nothing about how the book is distributed.

body.text: Track the percentage of the book that is not yet due, month by month. It is a better early warning than DSO, it cannot be flattered by a single large collection at month end, and anyone in the business can understand it.

children.text: Two Metrics Worth More Than DSO

body.latex: \text{Days Beyond Terms} = \frac{\sum (\text{Bucket Amount} \times \text{Average Days Overdue})}{\text{Total Receivables}}
body.caption: How late the book is, on average, beyond the terms you agreed
Collection Effectiveness Index: what share of collectable money you actually collected

children.text: For Sunrise Ceramics, days beyond terms works out to 36.98 days. The collection effectiveness index, using opening receivables of ₹52 crore and credit sales of ₹180 crore, is 84.47%. A business collecting well runs above 90%. Below 80% means the collection process, not the credit policy, is the problem.

body.label: Why the tail matters so much
body.context: Industry collection experience consistently shows recovery rates dropping sharply after 90 days and again after a year. An invoice that is two years old is usually a dispute, an insolvency, or a customer who has decided not to pay.

children.text: The Collection Process

Most overdue money in Indian businesses is not lost to fraud or insolvency. It is lost to drift: nobody called, the invoice had the wrong purchase order number, the customer raised a quality issue that nobody closed, and by the time anyone escalated it, the relationship had gone quiet.

body.title: A collection calendar that runs itself

events.title: Invoice reaches the customer
events.description: Correct GST details, purchase order number, delivery challan reference and e-way bill. An incorrect invoice is the most common reason for a payment being parked, and it is entirely self-inflicted.

events.title: Confirm receipt and acceptance
events.description: A short call to confirm the material and the invoice are both accepted. Any dispute surfaces here, not on the due date.

events.title: Polite reminder
events.description: An automated email with the invoice and the due date. This single step moves a surprising share of payments.

events.title: Follow up the same day
events.description: If the payment has not come, call the same day. Waiting a week teaches the customer that the due date is negotiable.

events.title: Escalate one level
events.description: From accounts to the purchase manager, with a statement of account attached. Log the reason given.

events.title: Stop further dispatches
events.description: Automatic under the credit policy, with a documented approval required to override. This is the step most companies skip and most regret.

events.title: Senior escalation and demand notice
events.description: Owner to owner, or sales head to purchase head, followed by a formal demand notice if there is no commitment.

events.title: Legal or recovery route
events.description: Decide deliberately: negotiate a settlement, issue a statutory notice, or move to the remedies below. Doing nothing is also a decision, and it is the expensive one.

body.text: The dispatch stop at day 30 is the only step with real leverage in it. Every reminder before it is a request. Once a customer knows that supply continues regardless of payment, the ageing schedule is the only thing that changes.

body.title: Fix the collection basics before blaming the customer
steps: Check that invoices carry the correct GST number, purchase order reference and delivery documentation before dispatch.
Confirm delivery and acceptance within a week, so disputes surface early rather than on the due date.
Send a statement of account to every credit customer monthly, and get balances confirmed at least once a year.
Maintain a dispute log with an owner and a closing date for each entry, since unresolved disputes are the most common hiding place for old balances.
Assign each customer to a named person for collections, rather than leaving it to whoever has time.
Review the ageing schedule with the sales team monthly, not the finance team alone.
Tie a portion of sales incentives to collection rather than to booked orders.

body.title: Which number would you track weekly?
body.question: A distribution business wants one receivables metric reviewed every week by the sales and finance teams together. Which is the most useful?
options: Debtor days computed from the latest month
The percentage of the book that is not yet due, and the rupee value over 90 days
The bad debt provision as a percentage of sales
body.explanation: Total receivables rise with sales and say little. Debtor days are a monthly average that hides the tail. The share of the book that is current, read alongside the value beyond 90 days, tells you both the health and the damage, and both are actionable this week.

children.text: Provisioning: Putting a Number on the Damage
Once a book is aged, provisioning is arithmetic. Under Ind AS 109, companies use an
expected credit loss

approach, applying a loss rate to each bucket based on their own history. Smaller businesses do the same thing with a simpler policy. Either way, the discipline is the same: every bucket carries a rate, and the total is not a negotiation.

markDefs.definition: Expected credit loss. The provisioning approach under Ind AS 109, where a loss rate is applied to each ageing bucket based on past experience.

body.caption: A provision matrix applied to the book (₹ crore)

children.text: The provision of ₹3.66 crore is 6.31% of the book, and more than three quarters of it comes from the ₹7 crore that is over 90 days old. That is the whole argument for ageing in one line: 12.07% of the book carries most of the risk.

body.title: Compute a provision
body.prompt: A company has receivables of ₹42 crore aged as follows: ₹18 crore not due, ₹9 crore 1 to 30 days past due, ₹6 crore 31 to 60, ₹4 crore 61 to 90, ₹3 crore 91 to 180 and ₹2 crore over 180. Its loss rates by bucket are 0.5%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 30% and 65%. What is the total provision in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Bucket by bucket: 0.09, 0.18, 0.30, 0.40, 0.90 and 1.30, giving ₹3.17 crore. The oldest ₹5 crore of the book, just 12% of it, contributes ₹2.20 crore of the provision.

body.title: Two things to know about the published version

children.text: Since the 2021 amendments to Schedule III, listed and larger companies publish a trade receivables ageing schedule in their annual report using different buckets from the ones a collections team uses: less than six months, six months to one year, one to two years, two to three years, and more than three years, each split between undisputed and disputed, and between considered good and considered doubtful.

The disputed column is the one to read first. A large disputed balance sitting in the one to two year bucket usually means a commercial disagreement nobody has resolved, and it is far less likely to convert to cash than an undisputed balance of the same age.

On tax, a provision for doubtful debts is not deductible. The Income-tax Act, 2025 continues the long-standing position under section 36(1)(vii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, that a deduction is available only when a bad debt is actually written off as irrecoverable in the books. Provisioning is an accounting judgement; the write-off is the tax event.
When the Customer Simply Will Not Pay

columns.label: Commercial and quasi-legal
points: Negotiated settlement, often the fastest recovery with the largest discount
A formal demand notice from a lawyer, which resolves a meaningful share of cases on its own
Cheque dishonour proceedings under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act
Arbitration, where the contract has a clause for it
For registered micro and small suppliers, the facilitation council route for delayed payments

columns.label: Court and insolvency
points: A summary suit for a debt on a written contract, faster than an ordinary civil suit
An application under section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code as an operational creditor
The insolvency route needs a default of at least ₹1 crore, the threshold since 2020
It is powerful because it threatens control of the company, not just the money
It is also slow, public and expensive, so it is a last step and sometimes a negotiating lever

children.text: Two practical notes.
Section 138 proceedings

remain common because the threat of a criminal case concentrates attention, but courts are congested and the process takes years, so treat it as pressure rather than as recovery. And if your business is itself a registered micro or small enterprise, the facilitation council route under the MSME law is usually faster and cheaper than court, with statutory interest attached. That mechanism, and the 45-day rule behind it, is the subject of Chapter 5.

markDefs.definition: Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which makes dishonour of a cheque for insufficient funds a criminal offence.

body.title: The metric that hides the tail
body.textWithBlank: Two companies can report the same receivables total and the same ___ days while one has a clean book and the other has crores stuck beyond 90 days, which is why the ageing schedule matters more than the average.
body.explanation: Debtor days, or DSO, is an average across the whole book. Only the ageing schedule shows the distribution, and the oldest buckets carry almost all of the loss.

body.title: The dispute that appeared on day 55
body.scenario: A customer owing ₹1.4 crore, due 45 days ago, has gone quiet. When your collections executive finally reaches the purchase manager, he says three consignments had quality problems and the company is withholding payment until it is sorted out. Your plant records show no quality complaint was ever logged. The customer has been buying for three years and has always paid late but always paid. Your sales head wants to keep supplying while it gets resolved.
body.prompt: What would you do, in what order, and what would you change in the process afterwards?
body.modelAnswer:
Treat the dispute as real until proved otherwise, and treat the timing as information.

First, separate the disputed amount from the rest. Ask for the specific invoices and consignments in question. Almost always only part of the ₹1.4 crore is actually disputed, and the undisputed balance should be collected now, this week, without waiting for the quality question to close.

Second, put a clock on the dispute. Send a written summary of the alleged defects, ask for photographs, batch numbers and the rejection note, and offer a joint inspection within seven days. A genuine quality complaint survives this. A delaying tactic usually does not.

Third, apply the credit policy. Dispatches stop until the undisputed portion is paid, with the override requiring the same senior approval as any other exception. Supplying through a dispute removes the only leverage you have, and it also funds the customer's cash crunch if that is what this really is.

Fourth, check the pattern. A quality issue raised at day 55, never logged at delivery, from a customer who has always paid late, is a cash flow signal more often than a quality signal. Pull the GST filing status and look at the wider trade for news.

What to change afterwards: confirm delivery and acceptance within seven days of every dispatch, so a defect claim raised two months later has no standing, and maintain a dispute log where every entry has an owner and a closing date. Most old receivables in India are not refusals to pay. They are disputes nobody closed.

body.label: MSME delayed payment facilitation
body.description: If your business is a registered micro or small enterprise, this is where delayed payment cases against buyers are filed. Useful to know from both sides of the table, since your customers may use it against you.

body.text: Receivables do not go bad on the day a customer refuses to pay. They go bad quietly, one uncollected week at a time, while everyone assumes somebody else is following up.

points: The ageing schedule, not the receivables total or DSO, is the report that tells you where the risk sits.
Track the share of the book that is not yet due and the rupee value beyond 90 days, monthly at minimum.
Days beyond terms and the collection effectiveness index are sharper than DSO, and both are easy to compute.
Most overdue money is lost to process drift: wrong invoice details, unresolved disputes and no escalation, rather than to genuine default.
A collection calendar with a hard dispatch stop at 30 days past due is the only step with real leverage.
Provision by bucket using loss rates, in the spirit of the expected credit loss approach, and remember that only an actual write-off is deductible for tax.
Recovery routes range from settlement and demand notices to cheque dishonour proceedings, summary suits and insolvency, which needs a default of at least ₹1 crore.
